clinicalPearls: An age-specific epileptic encephalopathy of infancy, with onset usually in the first year of life and peaking around 4-8 months.
Spasms are brief, often symmetrical contractions producing sudden flexion or extension of the trunk and limbs, typically occurring in clusters especially on waking.
The full West syndrome triad comprises epileptic spasms, the EEG pattern of hypsarrhythmia, and arrest or regression of development.
Developmental regression or loss of previously acquired skills, including loss of social smile or visual attention, is a crucial and sometimes early sign.
Spasms are frequently mistaken for colic, startle, or normal infant movements, causing dangerous delays in diagnosis.
An urgent EEG is essential; hypsarrhythmia is a chaotic, high-amplitude, disorganised interictal pattern that supports the diagnosis.

Many cases have an identifiable underlying cause such as a structural brain abnormality, tuberous sclerosis, genetic or metabolic disease, or perinatal injury, so investigation for aetiology is important.
Rapid initiation of effective treatment is critical, as prompt control of spasms and resolution of hypsarrhythmia is associated with better developmental outcomes.
reference.pathophysiology: Infantile spasms represent an age-dependent epileptic encephalopathy in which diverse insults to the developing brain converge on a common electroclinical expression. Structural, genetic, metabolic, or acquired abnormalities disrupt the maturing cortical and subcortical networks during a vulnerable developmental window, producing the hypersynchronous discharges seen as hypsarrhythmia and the characteristic spasms. The ongoing epileptic activity itself further disrupts normal brain development, contributing to the associated cognitive and developmental regression.
additionalDifferentials: Other early-onset epileptic encephalopathies (e.g. Ohtahara syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: Urgent EEG, ideally capturing sleep, to identify hypsarrhythmia
MRI brain to detect structural or malformative causes
Skin examination and evaluation for tuberous sclerosis
Metabolic and genetic testing to establish an underlying aetiology
Developmental assessment to document baseline and progress
Fundoscopy and ophthalmological review where indicated
redFlags: New clusters of spasms in an infant require urgent EEG and prompt treatment (EMERGENCY)
Developmental regression or loss of acquired milestones
Delay between symptom onset and treatment, which worsens prognosis
Signs suggesting an underlying structural, metabolic, or genetic disorder
Evolution to other seizure types or epileptic encephalopathy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is variable and strongly influenced by the underlying cause and by how quickly spasms and hypsarrhythmia are controlled; delayed treatment and identifiable structural or genetic causes are associated with worse developmental outcomes, while prompt effective therapy in previously normal infants offers the best chance of favourable development.
pitfalls: Dismissing spasms as colic, reflux, or benign startle and delaying EEG
Failing to appreciate developmental regression as a warning sign
Not pursuing a thorough search for an underlying cause
Delaying initiation of effective therapy, which reduces the chance of good outcome
Under-recognising subtle spasms occurring in clusters around sleep transitions
management: Start first-line hormonal therapy with ACTH or a high-potency oral corticosteroid such as prednisolone promptly to achieve rapid resolution of spasms and hypsarrhythmia
Use vigabatrin as first-line therapy, particularly when tuberous sclerosis is the underlying cause
Treat the identified aetiology, including surgery for a focal structural lesion and specific therapy for treatable metabolic causes such as a pyridoxine trial
Confirm response with repeat EEG to document resolution of hypsarrhythmia, since prompt control improves developmental outcome
Monitor vigabatrin-treated infants for visual field and retinal toxicity and monitor corticosteroid adverse effects such as hypertension, infection and glucose disturbance
Provide developmental surveillance and early intervention given the risk of regression
Refer urgently to paediatric neurology and offer genetic and metabolic evaluation with counselling where a heritable cause is identified
